rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: The principal branch of \(\cos^{-1} x\) is :
rows.solution: By convention \(\cos^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(\cos\) restricted to \(\left[0, \pi\right]\). On that interval \(\cos x\) decreases steadily from \(\cos 0 = 1\) to \(\cos \pi = -1\), so it is one-one there and takes every value of the range \([-1, 1]\) exactly once — which is precisely what an inverse needs. Hence the principal branch is \(\left[0, \pi\right]\). (The interval \(\left[\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right]\) cannot be used at all, since \(\cos\) returns to \(0\) at both ends and so is not one-one on it; \(\left[\pi, 2\pi\right]\) and \(\left[2\pi, 3\pi\right]\) are one-one but are not the branch the convention selects.)

rows.stem: If \(f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1 - \sin^3 x}{3\cos^2 x}, & \text{for } x \ne \frac{\pi}{2} \\ k, & \text{for } x = \frac{\pi}{2} \end{cases}\) is continuous at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\), then the value of k is :
rows.solution: Continuity at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) requires \(k = f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \lim_{x \to \pi/2} \frac{1 - \sin^3 x}{3\cos^2 x}\). Both parts vanish at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\), so factor first: \(1 - \sin^3 x = (1 - \sin x)\left(1 + \sin x + \sin^2 x\right)\) and \(3\cos^2 x = 3\left(1 - \sin^2 x\right) = 3(1 - \sin x)(1 + \sin x)\). For \(x \ne \frac{\pi}{2}\) the factor \((1 - \sin x)\) is non-zero and cancels, leaving \(\frac{1 + \sin x + \sin^2 x}{3(1 + \sin x)}\). As \(x \to \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\sin x \to 1\), so the limit is \(\frac{1 + 1 + 1}{3(1 + 1)} = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\). Hence \(k = \frac{1}{2}\).

rows.stem: If the direction cosines of a line are \(\lambda, \lambda, \lambda\), then \(\lambda\) is equal to :
rows.solution: Direction cosines of any line satisfy \(l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1\). Here \(l = m = n = \lambda\), so \(3\lambda^2 = 1\), giving \(\lambda^2 = \frac{1}{3}\) and \(\lambda = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Both signs are genuine, because a line has two opposite senses: \(\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\) and \(\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\) are direction cosines of the same line. So \(\lambda = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\); the single-signed values \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) are each only half the answer, and \(1\) is impossible since it would force \(3\lambda^2 = 3\).

rows.stem: If \(\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & x & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 3x \end{vmatrix} = -57\), the product of the possible values of x is :
rows.solution: Expand the determinant along the first column: \(\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & x & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 3x \end{vmatrix} = -1\left(3x^2 - 3\right) - 1\left(6x - 12\right) + 0 = -3x^2 - 6x + 15\). Setting this equal to \(-57\) gives \(-3x^2 - 6x + 15 = -57\), i.e. \(-3x^2 - 6x + 72 = 0\), i.e. \(x^2 + 2x - 24 = 0\). For a quadratic \(x^2 + bx + c = 0\) the product of the roots is \(c\), so the product of the possible values of \(x\) is \(-24\). (Explicitly the roots are \(x = 4\) and \(x = -6\), and \(4 \times (-6) = -24\).)

rows.stem: \(\int e^x (\cos x - \sin x)\, dx\) is equal to :
rows.solution: The integrand has the form \(e^x\left[f(x) + f'(x)\right]\) with \(f(x) = \cos x\), because \(f'(x) = -\sin x\). Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^x f(x)\right) = e^x\left[f(x) + f'(x)\right]\), the standard result \(\int e^x\left[f(x) + f'(x)\right]dx = e^x f(x) + C\) applies and gives \(e^x \cos x + C\). Checking directly, \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^x \cos x\right) = e^x \cos x - e^x \sin x = e^x(\cos x - \sin x)\), which is the integrand. So the value of the integral is \(e^x \cos x + C\).

rows.stem:
The integrating factor of the differential equation

\(\frac{dy}{dx} + y \tan x - \sec x = 0\) is :
rows.solution: Put the equation in the standard linear form \(\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\): here \(\frac{dy}{dx} + y\tan x = \sec x\), so \(P = \tan x\). The integrating factor is \(e^{\int P\,dx} = e^{\int \tan x\,dx} = e^{\log|\sec x|} = \sec x\). So the integrating factor is \(\sec x\). (Note \(\log \sec x\) is the integral \(\int \tan x\,dx\) itself, not the integrating factor, which is its exponential.)

rows.stem: Using matrices and determinants, find the value(s) of k for which the pair of equations \(5x - ky = 2\); \(7x - 5y = 3\) has a unique solution.
rows.solution:
Write the pair as \(AX = B\), with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -k \\ 7 & -5 \end{bmatrix}\), \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\). The system has a unique solution precisely when \(A\) is invertible, that is when \(|A| \ne 0\).

Here \(|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 5 & -k \\ 7 & -5 \end{vmatrix} = 5(-5) - (-k)(7) = -25 + 7k\).

So the condition is \(-25 + 7k \ne 0\), i.e. \(k \ne \frac{25}{7}\). Hence the pair of equations has a unique solution for every \(k \in \mathbb{R} - \left\{\frac{25}{7}\right\}\).

rows.stem: Find the local maxima and local minima of the function \(f(x) = \frac{8}{3}x^3 - 12x^2 + 18x + 5\).
rows.solution:
\(f(x) = \frac{8}{3}x^3 - 12x^2 + 18x + 5\), so \(f'(x) = 8x^2 - 24x + 18 = 2\left(4x^2 - 12x + 9\right) = 2(2x - 3)^2\).

For critical points put \(f'(x) = 0\): \(2(2x - 3)^2 = 0\) gives the single value \(x = \frac{3}{2}\).

Now \(2(2x - 3)^2 \ge 0\) for every real \(x\), so \(f'(x)\) is positive on both sides of \(x = \frac{3}{2}\) and vanishes only at that one point — it does not change sign as \(x\) crosses \(\frac{3}{2}\) from left to right. By the first derivative test, \(f\) has neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. (The function is in fact increasing on the whole of \(\mathbb{R}\), with \(x = \frac{3}{2}\) a stationary point of inflection.)

Let \(I = \int \frac{\cos x}{1 + \cos x + \sin x}\,dx\). Convert everything to half angles, using \(\cos x = \cos^2\frac{x}{2} - \sin^2\frac{x}{2}\), \(1 + \cos x = 2\cos^2\frac{x}{2}\) and \(\sin x = 2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}\):

\(I = \int \frac{\cos^2\frac{x}{2} - \sin^2\frac{x}{2}}{2\cos^2\frac{x}{2} + 2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}}\,dx\).

The numerator factors as \(\left(\cos\frac{x}{2} - \sin\frac{x}{2}\right)\left(\cos\frac{x}{2} + \sin\frac{x}{2}\right)\) and the denominator as \(2\cos\frac{x}{2}\left(\cos\frac{x}{2} + \sin\frac{x}{2}\right)\). Cancelling the common factor,

\(I = \int \frac{\cos\frac{x}{2} - \sin\frac{x}{2}}{2\cos\frac{x}{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\int\left(1 - \tan\frac{x}{2}\right)dx\).

Since \(\int \tan\frac{x}{2}\,dx = -2\log\left|\cos\frac{x}{2}\right|\),

\(I = \frac{1}{2}\left[x + 2\log\left|\cos\frac{x}{2}\right|\right] + C\).

rows.stem: Consider the experiment of tossing a coin. If the coin shows head, toss it again; but if it shows a tail, then throw a die. Find the conditional probability of the event A : 'the die shows a number greater than 3' given that B : 'there is at least one tail'.
rows.solution:
Because the second stage depends on the first, list the sample space as \(S = \{HH,\ HT,\ T1,\ T2,\ T3,\ T4,\ T5,\ T6\}\), where \(Ti\) means 'tail, then the die shows \(i\)'. The outcomes are not equally likely: \(P(HH) = P(HT) = \frac{1}{2}\times\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}\), while \(P(Ti) = \frac{1}{2}\times\frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}\) for each \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\).

Here \(A = \{T4, T5, T6\}\) and \(B = \{HT, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6\}\), so \(A \cap B = \{T4, T5, T6\}\).

\(P(A \cap B) = 3 \times \frac{1}{12} = \frac{3}{12} = \frac{1}{4}\) and \(P(B) = \frac{1}{4} + 6 \times \frac{1}{12} = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{4}\).

Hence \(P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{1/4}{3/4} = \frac{1}{3}\).

rows.stem:
The probability distribution of a random variable X is given as :

| X | 1 | 2 | 3 | \(2\lambda\) | \(3\lambda\) | \(4\lambda\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P(X) | \(\frac{11}{30}\) | \(\frac{1}{15}\) | \(\frac{1}{10}\) | \(\frac{3}{10}\) | \(\frac{1}{15}\) | \(\frac{1}{10}\) |

(i) Calculate \(\lambda\), if \(E(X) = 3{\cdot}2\).

(ii) Find \(P(X > 1)\).
rows.solution:
(i) \(E(X) = \sum x\,P(x) = 1\left(\frac{11}{30}\right) + 2\left(\frac{1}{15}\right) + 3\left(\frac{1}{10}\right) + 2\lambda\left(\frac{3}{10}\right) + 3\lambda\left(\frac{1}{15}\right) + 4\lambda\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\).

Taking \(30\) as the common denominator, the constant part is \(\frac{11 + 4 + 9}{30} = \frac{24}{30}\) and the \(\lambda\) part is \(\frac{18\lambda + 6\lambda + 12\lambda}{30} = \frac{36\lambda}{30}\), so \(E(X) = \frac{24 + 36\lambda}{30}\).

Given \(E(X) = 3{\cdot}2 = \frac{96}{30}\), we get \(24 + 36\lambda = 96\), so \(36\lambda = 72\) and \(\lambda = 2\).

(ii) With \(\lambda = 2\) the values taken by \(X\) are \(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8\), so the event \(X > 1\) is everything except \(X = 1\). Hence \(P(X > 1) = 1 - P(X = 1) = 1 - \frac{11}{30} = \frac{19}{30}\).

(As a check, the six given probabilities do add to \(1\): \(\frac{11}{30} + \frac{2}{30} + \frac{3}{30} + \frac{9}{30} + \frac{2}{30} + \frac{3}{30} = 1\).)

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following Linear Programming Problem graphically :

Minimise \(Z = 3x + 5y\)

subject to the constraints

\(x + 2y \ge 10\)

\(x + y \ge 6\)

\(3x + y \ge 8\)

\(x, y \ge 0\)

Evaluate :

\(\int\limits_0^{\pi/4} \frac{\sin x \cos x}{\cos^4 x + \sin^4 x}\, dx\)
rows.solution:
Let \(I = \int\limits_0^{\pi/4} \frac{\sin x \cos x}{\cos^4 x + \sin^4 x}\,dx\).

Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^4 x\), which is non-zero throughout \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right]\):

\(I = \int\limits_0^{\pi/4} \frac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1 + \tan^4 x}\,dx\).

Put \(t = \tan^2 x\), so that \(dt = 2\tan x \sec^2 x\,dx\), i.e. \(\tan x \sec^2 x\,dx = \frac{dt}{2}\), and \(1 + \tan^4 x = 1 + t^2\). The limits transform as \(x = 0 \Rightarrow t = 0\) and \(x = \frac{\pi}{4} \Rightarrow t = 1\). Hence

\(I = \frac{1}{2}\int\limits_0^1 \frac{dt}{1 + t^2} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\tan^{-1} t\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - 0\right) = \frac{\pi}{8}\).

[CBSE marking scheme: the official answer for this part reads, in full, 'Due to printing error, the given function is not integrable. So full marks may be given for every attempt.' All 5 marks were awarded to every candidate, so there is no expected solution to reproduce. What follows explains why the printed integrand cannot be done, and then works the question that was almost certainly intended.]

Why it does not close. Note first that \(\log(x^2 + 1) - 2\log x = \log\frac{x^2 + 1}{x^2} = \log\left(1 + \frac{1}{x^2}\right)\). Taking \(x > 0\) and substituting \(u = \frac{1}{x}\), so that \(\frac{dx}{x^2} = -du\) and \(\sqrt{x^2 + 1} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + u^2}}{u}\), the integral becomes \(-\int \frac{\sqrt{1 + u^2}\,\log\left(1 + u^2\right)}{u}\,du\). Putting \(s = \sqrt{1 + u^2}\) turns this into \(-2\int\left(1 + \frac{1}{s^2 - 1}\right)\log s\,ds\), and while \(\int \log s\,ds\) is elementary, \(\int \frac{\log s}{s^2 - 1}\,ds\) is a dilogarithm and is not. So no amount of rearranging will produce an answer in the functions of the syllabus.

The intended question. What went to press wrongly is the power of \(x\): with \(x^4\) in the denominator the substitution closes at once. For \(\int \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}\left[\log(x^2 + 1) - 2\log x\right]}{x^4}\,dx\), write \(\frac{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}{x^4} = \frac{1}{x^3}\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{x^2}}\) and put \(t = 1 + \frac{1}{x^2}\), so \(dt = -\frac{2}{x^3}\,dx\), i.e. \(\frac{dx}{x^3} = -\frac{dt}{2}\), while the bracket is exactly \(\log t\). The integral becomes

\(-\frac{1}{2}\int \sqrt{t}\,\log t\,dt\).

Integrating by parts with \(\log t\) as the first function, \(\int t^{1/2}\log t\,dt = \frac{2}{3}t^{3/2}\log t - \frac{2}{3}\int t^{1/2}\,dt = \frac{2}{3}t^{3/2}\log t - \frac{4}{9}t^{3/2}\), so

\(-\frac{1}{2}\int \sqrt{t}\,\log t\,dt = -\frac{1}{3}t^{3/2}\log t + \frac{2}{9}t^{3/2} + C = \left(\frac{x^2 + 1}{x^2}\right)^{3/2}\left[\frac{2}{9} - \frac{1}{3}\log\frac{x^2 + 1}{x^2}\right] + C\).

(That the intended denominator was \(x^4\) is an inference from the structure of the problem, not something CBSE states; the marking scheme records only that the function as printed is not integrable.)
